extracted.intended_audience: scholars, graduate students, and researchers in the history of mathematics and history of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and chapter outlines for composing scholarly chapters on the cultural history of mathematics across antiquity, the medieval age, and early modern Europe. Emphasizes themes, categories of problems, professional contexts, representational practices, and technological links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of mathematics (practical, theoretical, recreational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient verbal and visual depictions of mathematics included activities involving mathematical skills and individuals identified as mathematicians; mathematics is represented as practical, theoretical (or philosophical), and recreational (including riddles and games).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how mathematics functioned in wider culture and society, how various audiences displayed mathematical knowledge, and how practical desirability of calculations contrasted with special intellectual training. Examples: legendary accounts of problems and solutions; people took pleasure in displaying mathematical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branch-terms carry other (non-mathematical) meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms for branches of mathematics (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, harmonics, logistik¯e, stereometry, spherics) also carried other meanings (measurement of earth, knowledge of stars, musical theory), which color representations of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing texts, attend to semantic range of technical terms (example: Aristophanes' joke whether 'geometry' refers to measuring a farm or the entire Earth) and how non-mathematical meanings affect portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and genre affect mathematical representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many texts that portray mathematics and mathematicians were not written by mathematicians (e.g., Plato); genre (dialogue, Socratic model) shapes the presentation of mathematical problems and their philosophical framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish authors' purposes (philosophical vs mathematical) and how genre conventions (dialogue, silence of the mathematician character) influence depiction and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-cultural, periodized scope (CSAPGL emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume frames a culturally balanced view of global mathematics in surviving literate mathematical traditions primarily in Chinese, Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian, Greek, and Latin (CSAPGL), while noting but not fully treating other regional traces (Americas, sub-Saharan Africa, Polynesia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly delimit scope and justify inclusions/exclusions; discuss interactions with adjacent literate traditions (vernaculars, bilingual contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-cultural spread of decimal place-value numerals and arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the cross-cultural spread of decimal place-value numerals and associated arithmetic techniques, rival systems they paralleled/replaced, vernacular arithmetic education, vocational requirements, and the role of zero as a written symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat creation, spread, and absorption into everyday numeracy; examine introduction of zero (different lexical/functional forms in Chinese: kong vs ling), and transmission via paper and other technologies (India → Arab → Latin/Greek).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and professional contexts of medieval mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary professional contexts included astrology, commerce, surveying, architecture, construction, state/local engineering projects, and administrative computation; these contexts shaped mathematical practice and demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate education/training, status and support (patronage, salaries, business returns), demographics of practitioners, venues of work, and the effect of public attitudes on professional operations and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrices of innovation (categories of problems driving mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovations can be specified using categories of problems that drove research: computation with known quantities, computation with unknown quantities, properties of numbers, enumeration/combinatorics, properties of figures, solutions of triangles/trigonometry, refinement of approximate solutions, and mathematics of infinitely large/small quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these matrices to trace how problem-types provoked new techniques; give cross-cultural examples (Chinese simultaneous equations, Indian indeterminate equations, Islamic emphasis on primality), and link problem types to social/cultural incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for facilitating computation with known quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods include classical prosthaphairesis in trigonometry, function tables, arithmetic techniques, sophisticated place-value computation methods (decimal and sexagesimal), and encoded tables for rapid retrieval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document algorithmic and tabular devices used to speed computation and practical examples (root extraction, printed/verbal encodings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for facilitating computation with unknown quantities (algebraic methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes methods now called algebra, linear algebra, indeterminate equations, classification schemes for equations and algorithms for solving higher-order and multivariable problems; examples across traditions (Chinese simultaneous equations, Indian indeterminate techniques, Arabic algebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight algorithmic forms, classification schemes, handling of algebraic sign and surds, and cross-cultural transmission (e.g., Hindu algebra adoption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation of properties of numbers (series, primality, harmonics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different traditions emphasized different numerical properties: Islamic/European heirs of Euclidean tradition pursued integer characteristics like primality and amicability, Sanskrit/Chinese traditions studied series and equation types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical work, note which numerical properties were prioritized and how that reflects cultural/disciplinary priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques of enumeration and combinatorics
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems of counting combinations appeared in diverse contexts: metrical patterns in Sanskrit verse, algorithms for enumerating Arabic words formed from root letters, Pascal-triangle-like organization of coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace algorithmic techniques and their applications across literary, linguistic, and mathematical domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of geometric figures and their applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient geometry provided foundations for study of shapes used both for modelling real phenomena (planetary orbits) and for abstract constructions (regular heptagon), with continued explorations and refinements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include examples of applied modelling and purely geometrical innovations; assess methods and transmission across traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solutions of triangles and trigonometry (planar and spherical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of methods relating triangle sides to angles and circular arcs, with origins in Hellenistic chord trigonometry and later Indian sine-based trigonometry; cross-fertilization between Indian, Greco-Islamic, and Chinese approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider astronomical motivations and the 360-degree legacy; examine spherical vs planar techniques and their chronological/geographical diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for refining approximate solutions (interpolation, iteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical computations (especially astronomical) used approximations (linear approximations, false position methods, iterative techniques); such methods were not always admitted by rigorous mathematical demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document numerical approximation methods across traditions and note debates about their acceptability as mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics of infinitely large and small quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual and practical treatments of infinitely repeatable/divisible processes (approximations of pi, enumerability, expressing very large numbers) informed medieval mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace uses of infinity concepts for extrapolation and approximation; evaluate representational and notational strategies for very large/small quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics and worldviews (geometry, divination, abstract concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics was intertwined with cosmological and philosophical outlooks: modifications in geometric models of the universe (two-sphere/Ptolemaic vs alternatives), celestial divination/astrology and calendric timekeeping, and abstract concepts (sacred shapes/numbers, periodicity, predictability, role of the divine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the relations between mathematical models and metaphysical/theological commitments; distinguish innovations unique to the medieval period vs earlier inheritances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical modelling and the boundary with spherical trigonometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Medieval Chinese mathematical focus included astronomical modeling and trigonometric-like techniques; there are debates whether some computational methods qualify as spherical trigonometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in retroactively applying modern technical labels; assess methods on their procedural content rather than later terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geomancy/astrology and culturally specific numerological practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese geomancy and astrology differed from European/African practices and often related to sexagenary cycles, magic squares, and numerical mysticism that diverged from legitimate mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between mystical/numerological practices and technical mathematical computation; document their interactions with official astronomical bureaus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map making and ground-distance measurement devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Medieval advances in cartography and devices for measuring ground distances (mechanical odometer in Han dynasty) are mathematical problems related to map-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link measurement technologies, instruments, and mathematical techniques used in surveying and mapping; contextualize within technological and cultural exchange (e.g., Jesuit maps later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics and technological change (instruments and practical applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey important advances in observational/navigational/timekeeping devices (astrolabe, armillary sphere, compass, clocks), architecture/construction/mechanics (practical geometry of stonemasons, tilings, ´silpa formulas), transport and military science (shipbuilding, fortifications), and applications in agriculture, manufacture, mining/metallurgy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the mathematical content of instruments and techniques, note the scholar/artisan divide, and recognize that some key material innovations were not necessarily mathematical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational practices and structuring of mathematical texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical treatises used titles, tables of contents, headlines, subdivisions, foliations, formulas, diagrams, and other organizational means; medium (handwriting, wood-block printing) and material carriers (parchment, papyrus, paper, birch bark, palm leaves) shaped representational practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how material media and textual organization influenced the form and transmission of mathematical knowledge (e.g., wood-block printing in East Asia vs manuscript cultures in West Asia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material carriers and their epistemic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Different materials (paper, parchment, vellum, birch bark, palm leaves, metals, silk, bamboo, stone) were used across regions and social strata; choice of medium affected accessibility, durability, cost, and the kinds of works produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing sources, consider the medium's role in intended audience (practical vs courtly works), preservation biases, and the kinds of mathematical content likely to be recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everyday numeracy and calculation methods (counters vs written numerals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal calculation methods in Europe: counters on calculating boards (associated with Roman numeration) and written calculations using Indo-Arabic numerals; these coexisted long before the decimal positional system fully supplanted counters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze numeracy in relation to devices, user needs, and occupational variation; use textbooks to study how numeracy was taught and used in daily/professional life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbooks as sources for everyday numeracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks (15th–17th centuries) are crucial for understanding techniques/devices for number problems, how people became numerate, and numeracy in daily life; the multiplicity and diversification of textbooks reflect heterogeneity of numerical skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use textbooks to compare technical content across social groups (shopkeeper vs international merchant) and regional sophistication of accounting techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodization and heterogeneity of mathematical practice (Early Modern turn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Modern period saw transition from medieval quadrivium to new analysis; diversity of practitioners (commentators, practitioners, artisans, Jesuits, university mathematicians) and spread of mathematical practice through printing, instruments, letters, and missions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When framing historical narratives, account for heterogeneity, multiple venues of practice, and technological and institutional factors that reshaped mathematical authority and dissemination.
